title: Buddy Gilmore and press-roll drumming
summary: Gilmore gave Moore work on Long Island and was a Baby Dodds-like drummer; Moore discusses press rolls and a Gene Krupa award signed for Zutty Singleton.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Let's key in on Bid Sid and some of these others. I asked you about Buddy Gilmore at one time, the great drummer who was with James Reese Europe. Did you meet him?
Yeah. When I met him, he was living on Long Island.
Did you meet him before the Depression or was it during the Depression?
That was down around during the time... Between '28 and '29, around there. I think it was during that time.
Moore (II) - 19

Because I didn't come to New York until '28. And he used to get jobs for me, get me jobs over in Long Island. He had so much work that he couldn't do it himself, so he called on me. He did a lot of singing and he played old-time drums, but people loved it.
About how old was he? Was he much older than you?

Yeah, he was older than I am. He must have been round about...probably 28 or 29 years old, I guess he was. Of course, I was way younger than that... [IF MR. MOORE WAS BORN IN 1900, HE WAS 28 OR 29 WHEN HE MET BUDDY GILMORE]
[END OF TAPE 2, SIDE A]

So Buddy Gilmore was a few years older than you. But what kind of person was he? I get the impression from reading about him that he was a nice individual, easy to get along with, and very accommodating as far as showing people little tricks about the drums and so forth.

Yeah, he was a mighty good drummer. And as you said, he used to get along great. He knew right from wrong. He knew how to hold his sticks. A lot of drummers play drums and don't know how to hold the sticks. Sometimes they
Moore (II) - 20

hold them wrong. It's like a trumpet player. A trumpet player blow, but they blow wrong. That's the reason why they have so much trouble with the lips. They don't blow right. You've got to keep your stomach in shape, cleaned out.
You said he knew how to hold the sticks. Were there any particular things that he used to do that impressed you?
He did a lot of press rolling, snare drumming.
I see.

He'd do a lot of that, press rolls. Like Big Sid Catlett would do a lot of press rolls. Cozy Cole did a lot of it, too. Baby Dodds did a lot of press rolling. Zutty Singleton did a lot of press rolling. And you had drummers in different... Most of them were different style of drummers...

Freddie Moore is showing us "The Professional Percussion Center Presents The Gene Krupa Award to Zutty Singleton, July 2nd, 1974." And you are... One of the signers of this award is Fred Moore. Grady Tate is also a signer, Mickey Roker, Baby Lovett, Sam Unio(?), Ray McKenzie, Roy Eldridge, Terry Clarke, Stanley Kaye... Uh-huh! Okay.
Moore (II) - 21
And how would you make a comparison of Buddy Gilmore's way of playing with, say, Big Sid or Baby Dodds?

Yeah, he was on Baby Dodds' kick, Buddy Gilmore was. He played somewhat like Baby Dodds, on the rim of the drums, and hit the things, the cowbell, tom-tom, you know... But he knew how to put them different things in different spots. He knew when to come in, you know.
